Sample Size Planning for the Coefficient of Variation Given the Goal of Accuracy in Parameter Estimation Approach to Sample Size Planning

Source: R/ss_aipe_cv.R
ss_aipe_cv.Rd

Takes a planning value of the population coefficient of variation and a desired confidence interval width, and returns the smallest sample size at which the interval of ci_cv is expected to be that narrow (Kelley, 2007). With assurance it returns the sample size of the published procedure of that article, at which the realized two-sided interval is that narrow with about the stated probability. The interval and the plan assume a normal population (see Details).

The population coefficient of variation may be given directly as true_cv or through true_mean and true_sd, in which case true_cv is taken as true_sd / true_mean. It must be positive.

Usage

ss_aipe_cv(
  true_cv = NULL,
  width = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  assurance = NULL,
  true_mean = NULL,
  true_sd = NULL,
  alpha_lower = NULL,
  alpha_upper = NULL
)

Arguments

true_cv

Population coefficient of variation the sample size is planned for (kappa in Kelley, 2007). The planner treats this value as the truth; ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity shows what the plan delivers when the truth (true_cv there) differs from the value planned with (supposed_cv there).

width

Desired (full) width of the confidence interval

conf_level

Confidence interval coverage; 1-Type I error rate. A level above .999999998, whose tail areas are below 1e-9, is refused (see "Small tail areas" in ci_nc_t)

assurance

Optional. The probability that the realized interval is no wider than width: a single number strictly between 0 and 1 (for example .80, .90, or .99). A value such as .50 may be used; it asks that the realized interval be no wider than width in about half of the studies that could be run, where the plan without assurance asks that the width at the expected value of the sample coefficient be no larger than width. Near .50 the realized probability can be several points below the request and the sample size can be one smaller than without assurance; see Details for the procedure and the numbers. Any other value is refused with a condition of class dmar_assurance_invalid. assurance cannot be given with alpha_lower = 0, a one-sided upper confidence bound (see Edge cases).

true_mean

Population mean, a positive number (specified with true_sd when true_cv is not specified)

true_sd

Population standard deviation, a positive number (specified with true_mean when true_cv is not specified)

alpha_lower

Type I error for the lower confidence limit, given with alpha_upper when conf_level is NULL: a single number that is at least 0 and below 1

alpha_upper

Type I error for the upper confidence limit. A nonzero tail area below 1e-9 is refused, as in ci_cv

Value

A data.frame with the columns term and value and one row, necessary_N, the planned sample size, with or without assurance.

Details

Estimand and interval. The quantity planned for is the population coefficient of variation \(\kappa = \sigma / \mu\) of a normal population with a positive mean, estimated from \(N\) independent observations by \(k = s / M\). The interval is the one ci_cv reports, from the noncentral t distribution of \(\sqrt{N} / k\), two-sided at conf_level (or with the tail areas alpha_lower and alpha_upper when conf_level is NULL).

The expected-width plan. At each candidate sample size \(N\) the width is evaluated at the value Kelley (2007, Equation 3) gives for the expected value of the sample coefficient of variation given true_cv and \(N\), $$E[k \mid \kappa, N] \approx \kappa \left[1 - \frac{1}{4(N - 1)} + \frac{\kappa^2}{N} + \frac{1}{2(N - 1)^2}\right],$$ and the smallest \(N\) whose width at that value is no larger than width is returned. The expression is the approximation of Sokal and Braumann (1980, p. 51, Expression 3) for normal data. It stops at the third-order term and is above the expected value at small \(N\): for a coefficient of .25, by 3.1 percent at \(N = 5\), 0.6 percent at \(N = 10\), and 0.1 percent at \(N = 20\). The function keeps it because the published tables were computed with it. The search starts at \(N = 4\). The interval is computed exactly; for how this relates to the sample sizes tabled in Kelley (2007), see The published tables below.

The width of the interval is not a linear function of the sample coefficient of variation, so the width at the value of Equation 3 is not exactly the expected width. Over 62 conditions (coefficients of variation of .05 to .50, widths of .025 to .20, and confidence levels of .90, .95, and .99, with plans from 5 to 1,500) the returned \(N\) was the smallest \(N\) with an expected width no larger than width in 47 and one smaller in 15; where it was one smaller the expected width exceeded width by at most 0.7 percent.

The assurance step. With assurance the function runs the computation that produced the tables of Kelley (2007). At the expected-width sample size \(N_0\) it finds \(\kappa_\gamma\), the value that the sample coefficient exceeds with probability 1 - assurance, from the noncentral t distribution of Equation 5 of the article. It then takes the value of Equation 3 at \(\kappa_\gamma\) and \(N_0\) as the planning value and runs the expected-width search for it, which applies Equation 3 to that value again at each \(N\). The quantile and the intervals are computed exactly (see ci_nc_t). The article's text (p. 759) describes the search as run for \(\kappa_\gamma\) itself. Recomputed with R's own noncentral t functions, as in 2007, the computation described here gives the printed value in 524 of the 528 assurance cells of Tables 1 to 3 (the other four are in the two rows that show a misprint), where the search for \(\kappa_\gamma\) itself gives the printed value in 365. The two computations give different plans in 160 cells.

The published tables. Kelley (2007) computed Tables 1 to 3 (pp. 760–762) with R's noncentral t distribution, which is a normal approximation above a noncentrality of 37.62. Here the noncentrality is \(\sqrt{N}/k\), which narrow intervals pass, and the function computes there exactly, so it does not return every printed value. Two rows of the tables show a misprint. Table 1 (90 percent confidence), assurance .80, width .125, coefficient of variation .40 prints 127, between 69 and 122 in its row; the procedure gives 93. Table 3 (99 percent confidence), assurance .80, width .010 prints 14,279; 28,321; 50,209; 38,120; and 82,817 for coefficients of variation of .30 to .50, which do not increase; the procedure gives 14,277; 20,473; 28,320; 38,118; and 50,207, so the printed 28,321 and 50,209 are its values for .40 and .50 (to within the approximation), one and two columns to the left of where they belong. Apart from the four misprinted cells (127; 28,321; 50,209; and 82,817), the function returns the printed value in 468 of the 788 cells, one to three fewer cases in 232, and one to three more in 88. It returns every printed value with a width of .125 or more at 90 and 95 percent confidence, the misprint aside, and 9 of the 120 with a width of .075 or less at 99 percent. The worked example of the article (pp. 759–760), a coefficient of variation of .25, a width of .10, and 99 percent confidence, gives 101, and 142 with an assurance of .99, where the article gives 99 and 141: at 99 the interval at the expected value is .1006 wide, and .0999 by the approximation.

The procedure is a close approximation and not an exact search, so the probability that the realized interval is no wider than width at the returned sample size is near assurance and not exactly it. In the 488 printed cells with an assurance and at most 5,000 cases that probability was .744 to .902 where .80 was requested (below .80 in 37 of 244 cells) and .9916 to .9997 where .99 was requested. Away from the published tables, and more so as the request falls toward .50, it can fall below the request: for a coefficient of variation of .22, a width of .09, a 95 percent interval, and an assurance of .60 the function returns 57, at which the probability is .587, and one more case gives .621. In 105 plans computed at 95 percent confidence (coefficients of variation from .05 to .50, widths of a quarter, a half, and three quarters of the coefficient) the probability was below the request by at most .038 for a request of .50, .036 for .55, .058 for .60, .032 for .70, and .001 for .80, and it was not below the request in any plan for .90 and .99. A request of .50 does not reproduce the plan without assurance: in 12 of the 15 plans it returned a sample size one smaller than the plan without assurance does, and for a coefficient of variation of .05 and a width of .0375 it returns 17, at which the probability is .462, where the plan without assurance returns 18. In the other direction, when width is close to true_cv and assurance is high the returned sample size can be well above the smallest sufficient one: for a coefficient of variation of .5, a width of .5, a 95 percent interval, and an assurance of .99 the function returns 57, and the probability reaches .99 at 37. ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity estimates the probability for any plan by simulation.

Populations that are not normal. The interval and the plan assume a normal population. With a skewed population the coverage of the interval departs from the stated level, and a larger sample does not repair it (see ci_cv). In 40,000 samples at each of the three plans for a coefficient of variation of .50, a width of .20, and 95 percent confidence (79 without assurance, 97 with an assurance of .80, and 142 with .99), coverage was .97 for a gamma population with that coefficient of variation, and for a lognormal one it was .915, .913, and .905, lowest at the largest plan. The proportion of intervals no wider than width was .55, .88, and 1.00 for the gamma population and .59, .84, and .99 for the lognormal one. For a normal population that probability, computed from the noncentral t distribution, is .53, .84, and 1.00.

Edge cases. When width is already met at \(N = 4\) the function returns 4. A width that no sample size reaches within 100,000 steps of the search stops with an error. With alpha_upper = 0 the interval is a one-sided lower confidence bound whose upper limit is infinite at every sample size, so no plan exists, and the call is refused at once with a condition of class dmar_argument_invalid. With alpha_lower = 0, an upper bound, the lower limit is 0 and the width is the bound itself, which comes down toward the coefficient of variation as \(N\) grows, so a width larger than true_cv can be planned without assurance. With assurance the call is refused, with class dmar_argument_invalid: the assurance step was written for a two-sided interval and does not give the requested probability for a bound. For a coefficient of variation of .2, a width of .25, conf_level = NULL, alpha_lower = 0, and alpha_upper = .05, where the plan without assurance is 37, the step gives 33, 91, and 219 for an assurance of .50, .80, and .90. The probability that the bound is no larger than the width is .470, .878, and .998 at those sizes, and the smallest sample sizes at which it reaches the request are 36, 74, and 98. With alpha_upper below .5 the bound at the value of Equation 3 stays above true_cv at every sample size the search can reach: over true_cv from .001 to 5 and \(N\) from 4 to 100,004 the smallest bound was 1.000006 times true_cv. (The value of Equation 3 is itself below true_cv when true_cv is below \(\sqrt{N(N - 3)} / (2(N - 1))\), which is .33 at \(N = 4\), .46 at \(N = 10\), and .49 at \(N = 20\), and approaches .5.) A width at or below true_cv is therefore never reached, and the call is refused at once, also with class dmar_argument_invalid. With a large coefficient of variation the first sample sizes of the search can be so small that the upper limit of the interval is infinite (at 99 percent confidence and a coefficient of .45, \(N = 4\) is one). An infinite interval is never narrow enough, so the search goes on, and the interval at the returned sample size is finite.

Comparison with MBESS. MBESS 3.4.0 and later evaluate the width at true_cv multiplied by \((1 + 1/(4N))\), the nearly unbiased estimate of Kelley (2007, Equation 4) applied to the population value, which is larger than true_cv where the expected value is smaller, and use R's approximation to the noncentral t beyond a noncentrality of 37.62. Their sample sizes are one larger than the tables in Kelley (2007) in many conditions, and up to three larger with assurance; for the worked example they are 100 and 142, where this function gives 101 and 142.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2016). Estimation of the coefficient of variation with minimum risk: A sequential method for minimizing sampling error and study cost. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(5), 627–648. doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279

Kelley, K. (2007). Sample size planning for the coefficient of variation from the accuracy in parameter estimation approach. Behavior Research Methods, 39(4), 755–766. doi:10.3758/BF03192966

Sokal, R. R., & Braumann, C. A. (1980). Significance tests for coefficients of variation and variability profiles. Systematic Zoology, 29(1), 50–66. doi:10.1093/sysbio/29.1.50

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 3 on confidence intervals for effect sizes.)

See also

ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity, cv

design_consequences for what a chosen design delivers: power, the Type S (sign) and Type M (exaggeration) errors of the significance filter, and the expected confidence interval width.

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# Suppose one wishes to have a confidence interval with an expected width of .10
# for a 99% confidence interval when the population coefficient of variation is .10.
ss_aipe_cv(true_cv = .1, width = .1, conf_level = .99)
#>  term        value
#>  necessary_N 20   
#> 
#> Confidence level: 99%

# The same planning problem parameterized by the population mean and standard
# deviation: true_mean = 10 and true_sd = 1 imply the same coefficient of variation, .10.
ss_aipe_cv(true_mean = 10, true_sd = 1, width = .1, conf_level = .99)
#>  term        value
#>  necessary_N 20   
#> 
#> Confidence level: 99%

# Ensuring that the confidence interval will be sufficiently narrow with a 99%
# certainty for the situation above.
ss_aipe_cv(true_cv = .1, width = .1, conf_level = .99, assurance = .99)
#>  term        value
#>  necessary_N 32   
#> 
#> Confidence level: 99%
